chapters.title: Dedication
paragraphs: MOST HONORABLE, MAGNIFICENT AND SOVEREIGN LORDS: convinced that only a virtuous citizen can offer his country honors it can rightfully accept, I have spent thirty years trying to make myself worthy of paying you some public tribute. Since this fortunate occasion partly makes up for what my efforts could not, I have allowed myself to consult here the zeal that moves me rather than the standing that should authorize me. Having had the good fortune to be born among you, how could I reflect on the equality nature established between human beings, and the inequality they themselves have introduced, without also reflecting on the deep wisdom by which both are combined in your state in the manner most in keeping with natural law, most favorable to society, to public order, and to individual happiness? In searching for the best rules common sense can lay down for the constitution of a government, I have been so struck to find them all already in force in yours that, even had I not been born within your walls, I would have felt it my duty to offer this portrait of human society to that people which, more than any other, seems to possess its greatest advantages and to have best guarded against its abuses.

If I had been able to choose where to be born, I would have chosen a society sized to the limits of human capacity—that is, to what can actually be well governed; one where each person can match his own role, so that no one is forced to delegate the duties entrusted to him; a state in which everyone knows everyone else, so that neither the hidden workings of vice nor the modesty of virtue could escape public notice and public judgment; and where the pleasant habit of seeing and knowing one another would make love of country mean love of fellow citizens rather than love of the land.

I would have wished to be born in a country where the interest of the sovereign and that of the people are one and the same, so that every movement of the political machinery would tend toward the general happiness. And since this is only possible when the sovereign and the people are the same person, it follows that I would have wished to be born under a wisely tempered democracy.

I would have wished to live and die free—that is, so bound by the laws that neither I nor anyone else could shake off their honorable yoke: the easy, salutary yoke that even the proudest necks bear all the more willingly because they were made to bear no other.

I would have wished, then, that no one inside the state could claim to be above the law, and that no outsider could dictate terms the state was forced to recognize. For whatever a government's constitution may be, if a single person within its jurisdiction is not subject to the law, all the rest are necessarily at his mercy. And if there is a national ruler inside and a foreign ruler outside, however they divide their authority, it is impossible for both to be properly obeyed or for the state to be well governed.

I would not have chosen to live in a newly founded republic, however excellent its laws, for fear that the government, perhaps framed differently than the moment required, would not match the new citizens or they it, and the state would risk being overthrown almost as soon as it was born. Liberty is like rich, hearty food or strong wine: it nourishes and fortifies robust constitutions that are used to it, but ruins and intoxicates the weak and delicate that are not. Peoples once accustomed to masters cannot do without them. If they try to shake off the yoke, they only drift further from freedom, since they mistake for liberty an unbridled license that is its exact opposite, and they nearly always manage, through their revolutions, to deliver themselves up to seducers who only make their chains heavier than before. The Roman people itself, the model for all free peoples, was wholly incapable of governing itself when it escaped from the oppression of the Tarquins. Debased by slavery and the demeaning tasks imposed on it, it was at first nothing but a stupid mob that had to be controlled and governed with the greatest wisdom, so that, gradually growing accustomed to the bracing air of liberty, minds that had been weakened or rather brutalized by tyranny could slowly acquire the moral strictness and steadfast spirit that eventually made it the most respected of peoples. I would therefore have sought, as my country, some peaceful and happy republic of an antiquity so deep it was lost in the night of time, one that had experienced only the kinds of shocks that revealed and strengthened the courage and patriotism of its people, and whose citizens, long used to a wise independence, were not merely free but worthy of being free.

I would have wished to choose myself a country shielded by a fortunate weakness from the brutal love of conquest, and secured by an even more fortunate location from the fear of being conquered by other states—a free city situated among several nations, none of which would have any interest in attacking it, while each would have an interest in keeping the others from doing so; in short, a republic with nothing to tempt the ambition of its neighbors, but able to count reasonably on their help when needed. It follows that a republican state so happily placed would have nothing to fear except from itself, and that if its members trained themselves in arms, it would be more to keep alive the military spirit and courage that suit free men and sustain their taste for liberty than out of any real need to defend themselves.

I would have sought a country in which the right to make laws was held by all the citizens, for who is better placed than they are to judge the conditions under which they should live together in the same society? Not that I would have approved of plebiscites like those of the Romans, where the leading men of the state and those most invested in its preservation were excluded from the deliberations on which its security often depended, and where, by the most absurd inconsistency, the magistrates were stripped of rights enjoyed by the humblest citizens.

On the contrary, I would have wished that, in order to prevent self-interested and ill-conceived projects and the kind of dangerous innovations that finally ruined the Athenians, no single person would be free to propose new laws at will; this right would belong exclusively to the magistrates. And even they should use it so cautiously, the people should be so reserved in giving consent, and the promulgation should be carried out with such solemnity, that before the constitution could be overturned there would be time enough for everyone to be convinced that it is above all the great age of laws that makes them sacred and venerable, that people quickly learn to despise laws they see altered daily, and that states which get used to neglecting their ancient customs under the pretext of improvement often introduce evils greater than the ones they are trying to remove.

I would have particularly avoided, as necessarily ill-governed, a republic in which the people, imagining they could do without magistrates—or at least leave them only a precarious authority—imprudently kept for themselves the running of civil affairs and the execution of their own laws. Such must have been the rough constitution of the earliest governments, just emerging from a state of nature, and this was another of the vices that brought down the Republic of Athens.

But I would have chosen a community in which the individuals, content to sanction their laws and decide the most important public affairs in general assembly on the recommendation of their leaders, had established respected courts, carefully distinguished the various branches, and elected, year by year, the most capable and upright of their fellow citizens to administer justice and govern the state. In short, a community in which the virtue of the magistrates bore witness to the wisdom of the people, and each class did honor to the other. If, in such a place, any unfortunate misunderstandings arose to disturb the public peace, even these intervals of blindness and error would bear the marks of moderation, mutual esteem, and a shared respect for the laws—sure signs and pledges of a reconciliation as lasting as it was sincere. Such, most honorable, magnificent and sovereign lords, are the advantages I would have sought in the country I would have chosen to be born in. And if providence had added to all this a beautiful setting, a temperate climate, fertile soil, and the loveliest countryside under heaven, then to complete my happiness I would have wished only for the peaceful enjoyment of all these blessings, living at peace in the sweet society of my fellow citizens, and, following their example, practicing toward them the duties of friendship, humanity, and every other virtue, so as to leave behind me the honorable memory of a good man and an upright and virtuous patriot.

But if, less fortunate or having grown wise too late, I had found myself reduced to ending an ailing and feeble life in some other climate, vainly regretting the peaceful repose I had thrown away through the imprudence of youth, I would at least have nourished the same feelings in my heart, even denied the chance to express them in my native country. Filled with a tender and disinterested love for my distant fellow citizens, I would have addressed them from the heart, something like this.

"My dear fellow citizens, or rather my brothers, since the ties of blood and of law unite nearly all of us, it gives me pleasure that I cannot think of you without at the same time thinking of all the blessings you enjoy, and of which none of you, perhaps, feels the value as deeply as I do, having lost them. The more I reflect on your civil and political condition, the less I can imagine that the nature of human affairs could allow a better one. In all other governments, when there is a question of securing the greatest good of the state, things never get beyond projects and ideas, or at best mere possibilities. But for you, your happiness is complete; you have only to enjoy it. To be made perfectly happy, you need nothing more than to know how to be satisfied with being so. Your sovereignty, won or recovered by the sword and maintained for two centuries by your courage and wisdom, is at last fully and universally recognized. Your borders are fixed, your rights confirmed, and your peace secured by honorable treaties. Your constitution is excellent, not only dictated by the deepest wisdom but guaranteed by great and friendly powers. Your state enjoys perfect tranquility. You have neither wars nor conquerors to fear; you have no master other than the wise laws you yourselves have made, administered by upright magistrates of your own choosing. You are neither rich enough to be enervated by softness and to lose, in the pursuit of trivial pleasures, the taste for real happiness and solid virtue, nor poor enough to need more outside help than your own industry can provide. Meanwhile, the precious privilege of liberty—maintained in great nations only by submitting to the most ruinous taxes—costs you almost nothing to preserve.

May a republic so wisely and happily constituted last forever, as an example to other nations and for the happiness of its own citizens! This is the only prayer you still need to make, the only precaution that remains to be taken. From here on it depends on you alone—not to be made happy, for your ancestors have already saved you that trouble, but to make that happiness lasting through the wisdom with which you enjoy it. Your preservation depends on your continued unity, your obedience to the laws, and your respect for those who serve them. If even the smallest trace of bitterness or distrust remains among you, hurry to root it out, as an accursed yeast that sooner or later must bring misfortune and ruin to the state. I beg you all to look into your hearts and to listen to the secret voice of conscience. Is there anyone among you who can find, anywhere in the world, a body more upright, more enlightened, and more honorable than your magistracy? Do not all its members set you an example of moderation, simplicity of manners, respect for the laws, and the most sincere harmony? Place, then, without reserve, in such wise superiors the salutary confidence that reason always owes to virtue. Remember that they are your own choice, that they justify that choice, and that the honors due to those whom you have elevated are necessarily yours as well, by reflection. None of you is so ignorant as not to know that when the laws lose their force and those who defend them their authority, security and liberty become impossible for everyone. So why hesitate to do cheerfully, and with proper confidence, what you would in any case be bound to do by your true interest, by duty, and by reason itself?

Never let a guilty and harmful indifference to the upkeep of the constitution lead you to ignore, when necessary, the prudent advice of the most enlightened and most zealous of your fellow citizens. Instead, let fairness, moderation, and firm resolve continue to govern everything you do, and show you to the whole world as the example of a brave and modest people, jealous of their honor and their liberty in equal measure. Be especially on guard, as the last piece of advice I will give you, against sinister interpretations and poisonous rumors, whose hidden motives are often more dangerous than the actions they target. A whole household will wake up and respond to the first alarm given by a good and trusty watchdog that only barks at the approach of thieves. But we come to hate the nuisance of those noisy yapping dogs that keep disturbing the public peace, whose constant ill-timed warnings make us tune them out at the very moments when they might really be necessary."

And you, most honorable and magnificent lords, the worthy and revered magistrates of a free people, allow me to offer you in particular my respect and homage. If there is a station in the world capable of conferring honor on those who hold it, it is undoubtedly the one in which virtue and talent together place a person—the one you have made yourselves worthy of, and to which your fellow citizens have elevated you. Their worth adds new luster to your own; and since you have been chosen, by men capable of governing others, to govern them, I cannot help regarding you as much superior to all other magistrates as a free people, and particularly the one you have the honor to lead, is superior in wisdom and reason to the populace of other states.

Allow me to cite one example for which better records ought to have survived, and one that will always be close to my heart. I cannot recall, without the sweetest emotion, the memory of that virtuous citizen to whom I owe my existence, and who often taught me, in my infancy, the respect that is due to you. I see him still, living by the work of his hands and feeding his soul on the most sublime truths. I see the works of Tacitus, Plutarch, and Grotius lying before him among the tools of his trade. Beside him stands his dear son, receiving, alas with too little benefit, the tender instructions of the best of fathers. But if the follies of youth made me forget his wise lessons for a while, I am at last happy to be conscious that, whatever inclination one may have to vice, it is not easy for an education in which love has played a part to be entirely wasted.

Such, my most honorable and magnificent lords, are the citizens, and even the ordinary inhabitants, of the state you govern. Such are those intelligent and sensible men of whom, under the names of workmen and the people, it is customary in other nations to hold a low and false opinion. My father, I confess with pleasure, was in no way distinguished among his fellow citizens. He was only what they all are; and yet, such as he was, there is no country in which his acquaintance would not have been sought after, and cultivated with profit, by men of the highest character. It would not become me—nor, thank heaven, is it at all necessary—to remind you of the regard such men have a right to expect from their magistrates, to whom they are equal in education and in the rights of nature and birth, and inferior only by their own will, by that preference they owe to your merit, and for granting which they can claim some sort of acknowledgment in return. With lively satisfaction I observe that the greatest candor and good will attend, in all your conduct toward them, the gravity that becomes the ministers of the law, and that you repay them just as well, by your esteem and attention, for the respect and obedience they owe to you. This conduct is not only just but prudent, since it tends, happily, to erase the memory of many unhappy events that ought to be buried in eternal oblivion. It is also all the wiser because it makes this generous and equitable people find pleasure in its duty, naturally love to honor you, and ensures that those who are most zealous in defending their own rights are at the same time the most willing to respect yours.

It should not be surprising that the rulers of a civil society have the welfare and glory of their communities at heart. But it is uncommonly fortunate for the peace of mankind when those who consider themselves the magistrates—or rather the masters—of a holier and more sublime country show some love for the earthly country that sustains them. I am happy to make so singular an exception in our favor, and to be able to rank, among its best citizens, those zealous keepers of the sacred articles of faith established by the laws, those venerable shepherds of souls whose powerful and engaging eloquence is all the better suited to carry the maxims of the gospel into people's hearts because they themselves are the first to put them into practice. Everyone knows how successfully the art of preaching is cultivated in Geneva. But people are so used to hearing clergymen preach one thing and practice another that few have any way of knowing how far the spirit of Christianity, holiness of conduct, severity toward themselves, and indulgence toward their neighbors actually prevail throughout the whole body of our ministers. It is perhaps given to the city of Geneva alone to produce the edifying example of so perfect a union between its clergy and its men of letters. It is largely on their wisdom, their well-known moderation, and their zeal for the state's prosperity that I build my hopes for its lasting tranquility. At the same time, I notice with pleasure mixed with surprise and reverence how thoroughly they reject the dreadful maxims of those accursed and barbarous men of whom history furnishes more than one example—men who, in order to defend the supposed rights of God (meaning their own interests), have been all the less sparing of human blood the more confident they were that their own, in particular, would always be respected.

I must not forget that precious half of the republic which makes the happiness of the other, and whose sweetness and prudence preserve its tranquility and virtue. Amiable and virtuous daughters of Geneva, it will always be your sex's lot to govern ours. Happy are we, so long as your chaste influence, exercised only within the bounds of marriage, is exerted for the glory of the state and the happiness of the public. It was this way that women commanded at Sparta, and this is how you deserve to command at Geneva. What man can be such a barbarian as to resist the voice of honor and reason coming from the lips of an affectionate wife? Who would not despise the vanities of luxury, on seeing the simple and modest dress which, lit by the radiance it borrows from you, seems most flattering to beauty? Your task is to perpetuate, by your gentle influence and your innocent and amiable rule, respect for the laws of the state and harmony among the citizens. It is yours to reunite divided families by happy marriages and, above all, to correct, by the persuasive sweetness of your lessons and the modest grace of your conversation, the extravagances our young people pick up in other countries—where, instead of the many useful things they could profit by, they bring home hardly anything besides a childish swagger and a ridiculous manner picked up among loose women, plus an admiration for some so-called grandeur and paltry rewards for being slaves, which can never come anywhere near the real greatness of liberty. Continue, then, always to be what you are, the chaste guardians of our morals and the sweet pledge of our peace, exerting on every occasion the privileges of the heart and of nature in the service of duty and virtue.

I flatter myself that I will never be proved wrong in building, on such a foundation, my hopes for the general happiness of the citizens and the glory of the republic. It must be admitted, however, that with all these advantages it will not shine with that dazzling luster by which most men's eyes are taken in—a childish and fatal taste for which is the deadliest enemy of happiness and liberty.

Let our dissolute youth go elsewhere to find light pleasures and long regrets. Let our self-appointed arbiters of taste admire elsewhere the grandeur of palaces, the beauty of carriages, sumptuous furniture, the pomp of public entertainments, and all the refinements of luxury and softness. Geneva boasts nothing but men; yet such a sight has a value of its own, and those who have a taste for it are well worth the admirers of all the rest.

Deign, most honorable, magnificent and sovereign lords, to receive with equal kindness this respectful testimony of the interest I take in your common prosperity. And if I have been so unfortunate as to be guilty of some indiscreet outburst in this warm effusion of my heart, I beg you to pardon me, and to attribute it to the tender affection of a true patriot and to the ardent and legitimate zeal of a man who can imagine for himself no greater happiness than to see you happy.
Most honorable, magnificent and sovereign lords, I am, with the most profound respect,
Your most humble and obedient servant and fellow citizen.
J. J. ROUSSEAU. Chambéry, June 12, 1754.

chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Of all human sciences, the most useful and the most imperfect, in my view, is the one that studies humankind. I will venture to say that the single inscription on the Temple of Delphi contained a precept more difficult and more important than anything in all the huge volumes the moralists have ever written. I consider the subject of this discourse one of the most interesting questions philosophy can propose, and unfortunately for us, one of the thorniest philosophers have to solve. For how can we know the source of inequality among human beings if we don't first know what human beings are? And how can a person hope to see himself as nature made him, through all the changes that the succession of times and circumstances must have produced in his original constitution? How can he distinguish what is fundamental to his nature from the changes and additions his circumstances and his progress have introduced into his primitive condition? Like the statue of Glaucus—so disfigured by time, sea, and storms that it looked more like a wild beast than a god—the human soul, altered in society by a thousand constantly recurring causes, by the acquisition of countless truths and errors, by changes in the body's constitution, and by the continual collision of the passions, has, so to speak, changed in appearance to the point of being almost unrecognizable. Instead of a being acting always from fixed and unchanging principles, instead of that heavenly and majestic simplicity its divine Author impressed on it, we now find only the deformed contrast of passion mistaking itself for reason, and of an understanding gone delirious.

It is still crueler that, as every advance the human species makes moves it further from its primitive state, the more discoveries we accumulate, the more we deprive ourselves of the means of making the most important one. In a sense, then, it is by our very study of man that we have put ourselves out of any condition to know him.

It is easy to see that it is in these successive changes in the human constitution that we must look for the original source of the differences that now distinguish people, who, it is agreed, are as naturally equal to one another as the animals of every kind were before physical causes introduced into some of them the varieties we now observe.

It is not, in fact, conceivable that these primary changes, however they arose, altered every individual of the species at the same time and in the same way. Naturally, while some grew better or worse, acquiring various good or bad qualities not inherent in their nature, others remained longer in their original condition. This was undoubtedly the first source of inequality among human beings—something it is far easier to demonstrate in these general terms than to assign with any precision to its actual causes.

My readers should therefore not imagine that I flatter myself with having seen what seems to me so difficult to see. I have here set out certain lines of reasoning and ventured a few conjectures, less in the hope of solving the problem than of throwing some light on it and reducing the question to its proper form. Others may easily go further along the same road, though no one will find it easy to reach the end. For it is no small undertaking to distinguish properly between what is original and what is artificial in our actual nature, or to form a true idea of a state that no longer exists, perhaps never existed, and probably never will exist—yet of which we need accurate ideas in order to judge our present condition properly. It would, in fact, take more philosophy than people imagine to determine exactly what precautions one should take in order to make solid observations on this subject. And it seems to me that a good solution to the following problem would not be unworthy of the Aristotles and Plinys of our day: what experiments would be needed to find the natural man, and how could those experiments be conducted within society?

Far from undertaking to solve this problem, I think I have considered the subject enough to venture to declare in advance that our greatest philosophers would not be too good to direct such experiments, nor our most powerful sovereigns to carry them out. We have very little reason to expect such a combination, especially attended with the perseverance, or rather the succession of intelligence and goodwill, that would be needed on both sides for success.

These investigations, so difficult to make and until now so little thought about, are nevertheless the only means we have left of clearing up a host of difficulties that hide from us the real foundations of human society. It is our ignorance of human nature that casts so much uncertainty and obscurity on the true definition of natural right. For the idea of right, as Burlamaqui says, and even more so the idea of natural right, are obviously ideas relative to the nature of man. It is therefore from man's nature itself, he goes on, from his constitution and his condition, that we must derive the first principles of this science.

We cannot help noticing, with surprise and revulsion, how little agreement there is among the various authors who have treated this great subject. Among the most serious writers, you can scarcely find two who think alike on it. Setting aside the ancient philosophers, who seem to have made it their business to contradict one another on the most basic principles, the Roman jurists subjected human beings and other animals indiscriminately to the same natural law, because under that name they considered the law nature imposes on herself rather than the law she prescribes to others—or rather because of the particular sense in which those jurists used the word law, by which they seem to have meant nothing more than the general relations established by nature between all living beings for their common preservation. The moderns, by contrast, take law to mean only a rule prescribed to a moral being—that is, an intelligent, free being considered in his relations with other beings—and therefore confine the jurisdiction of natural law to man, the only animal endowed with reason. But, defining this law each in his own way, they establish it on such metaphysical principles that even among us very few people are capable of grasping them, let alone of finding them on their own. So that the definitions of these learned men, while disagreeing about everything else, agree only in this: that it is impossible to grasp the law of nature, and therefore to obey it, without being a very subtle reasoner and a profound metaphysician. Which is to say, precisely, that mankind must have employed, in establishing society, a level of insight that is developed only with great difficulty, and by very few people, even within society itself.

Knowing so little of nature, and agreeing so poorly about the meaning of the word law, it would be very difficult for us to settle on a good definition of natural law. So all the definitions we find in books, in addition to their lack of uniformity, suffer from another flaw: they are drawn from many kinds of knowledge people don't naturally possess and from advantages they can have no idea of until they have already left the state of nature. Modern writers start by asking what rules it would be useful for people to agree on for the common good, and then give the name natural law to a collection of these rules, with no further proof than the good that would come of their being universally practiced. That, certainly, is a very convenient way of making definitions and explaining the nature of things through almost arbitrary conveniences.

But as long as we are ignorant of the natural man, it is in vain that we try to determine either the law originally prescribed to him or the law best suited to his constitution. All we can really know about this law is that, for it to be a law, the will of those it obliges must be able to submit to it knowingly; and for it to be natural, it must speak directly through the voice of nature.

Setting aside, then, all those scientific books that teach us only to see men as they have made themselves, and reflecting on the first and simplest operations of the human soul, I believe I can perceive in it two principles prior to reason: one strongly interesting us in our own welfare and self-preservation, the other inspiring a natural reluctance to see any sentient being—and especially any of our own species—suffer or die. From the concurrence and combination our minds are able to make of these two principles, without needing to bring in the principle of sociability, all the rules of natural right seem to me to flow—rules that reason is afterward forced to re-establish on other foundations once its successive developments have managed to smother nature itself.

Proceeding this way, we are not obliged to make a person into a philosopher before he is a person. His duties toward others are not dictated to him solely by the late lessons of wisdom, and as long as he does not resist the inner impulse of compassion, he will never do harm to another human being, or even to any sentient creature—except on those legitimate occasions when, his own preservation being at stake, he is obliged to put himself first. This method also settles the time-honored disputes about whether animals participate in natural law. For it is clear that, lacking intelligence and freedom, they cannot recognize this law; but since they share something of our nature through their capacity to feel, we may judge that they too ought to participate in natural rights, and that human beings owe them some sort of duty. In fact, if I am bound to do no harm to my fellow creatures, it seems to be less because they are rational than because they are sentient—and this quality, common to both humans and beasts, ought at the very least to entitle the latter not to be wantonly mistreated by the former.

This same study of original man, of his real needs, and of the fundamental principles of his duty, is besides the only good way to clear up the host of difficulties that arise concerning the origin of moral inequality, the true foundations of the body politic, the reciprocal rights of its members, and a thousand other equally important and ill-understood questions.

If we look at human society with a calm and disinterested eye, at first glance it seems to show us only the violence of the powerful and the oppression of the weak. The mind is shocked by the cruelty of the one or moved to lament the blindness of the other. And since nothing among human beings is less stable than those external relationships—produced more often by accident than by wisdom and called weakness or power, wealth or poverty—human institutions look at first glance as if they were built on shifting sand. Only by examining them closely, only after clearing away the dust and sand that surround the edifice, do we perceive the unshakable foundation on which it rests and learn to respect what it is built on. Now, without a serious study of man, his natural faculties, and their successive development, we will never manage to make these distinctions, or to separate, in the actual constitution of things, what divine will has done from what human art has tried to do. The political and moral investigations to which the important question I am examining gives rise are therefore useful in every respect, and the hypothetical history of governments is a lesson instructive to humankind in every way.

In considering what we would have become if left to ourselves, we should learn to bless him whose gracious hand, correcting our institutions and giving them an unshakable footing, has prevented the disorders that would otherwise have arisen from them, and made our happiness spring from the very means that seemed bound to fill us with misery.
Quem te deus esse / Jussit, et humanâ quâ parte locatus es in re, / Disce. (Persius, Satire iii, 71.)
A DISCOURSE
ON THE ORIGIN AND FOUNDATION OF THE INEQUALITY OF MANKIND

It is of man that I have to speak, and the question I am examining shows me that I am about to speak to human beings. For questions of this sort are not put forward by those afraid to honor the truth. I shall therefore confidently defend the cause of humanity before the wise men who invite me to do so, and I will not be displeased with myself if I prove worthy of my subject and of my judges.

I conceive that there are two kinds of inequality among the human species. One, which I call natural or physical, is established by nature and consists in the differences of age, health, bodily strength, and the qualities of mind or soul. The other, which can be called moral or political inequality, depends on a kind of convention and is established, or at least authorized, by the consent of human beings. This latter consists of the different privileges that some enjoy at the expense of others—being richer, more honored, more powerful than others, or even able to make them obey.

It is useless to ask what is the source of natural inequality, because the answer is contained in the simple definition of the word. It is even more useless to ask whether there might be some essential link between the two kinds of inequality, since that would be asking, in other words, whether those who command are necessarily worth more than those who obey, and whether strength of body or mind, wisdom or virtue, are always found in the same individuals in proportion to their power or wealth—a question perhaps fit to be debated among slaves within hearing of their masters, but unfitting for reasonable and free men in search of the truth.

What, then, is the precise subject of this discourse? To mark, in the progress of things, the moment when right took the place of violence and nature became subject to law; to explain by what chain of miracles the strong could resolve to serve the weak, and the people to purchase an imagined repose at the price of real happiness.

The philosophers who have examined the foundations of society have all felt the necessity of going back to the state of nature, but none of them has reached it. Some have not hesitated to credit man in that state with the idea of just and unjust, without bothering to show that he must have had such an idea, or that it could even have been of any use to him. Others have spoken of the natural right that each person has to keep what belongs to him, without explaining what they meant by belongs. Others again, beginning by giving the strong authority over the weak, immediately produced government, without considering the time that must have passed before the meaning of words like authority and government could even exist among human beings. In short, all of them, constantly talking about needs, greed, oppression, desires, and pride, have transferred to the state of nature ideas they picked up in society. They spoke of savage man and they described civilized man. It has not even occurred to most of our writers to doubt whether the state of nature ever existed; though it is plain, from a reading of the sacred books, that the first man, having received understanding and commandments directly from God, was not himself in that state, and that, if we extend to the writings of Moses the credit every Christian philosopher owes them, we must deny that even before the Flood human beings were ever in the pure state of nature—unless they had fallen back into it through some extraordinary event, a paradox very embarrassing to defend and entirely impossible to prove.

Let us, then, begin by setting all the facts aside, since they don't touch the question. The investigations we may enter into on this subject should not be taken as historical truths, but only as hypothetical and conditional reasonings, better suited to clarify the nature of things than to demonstrate their actual origin—much like the hypotheses our physicists put forward every day about the formation of the world. Religion commands us to believe that, God Himself having drawn human beings out of the state of nature immediately after creation, they are unequal because He willed them to be so. But religion does not forbid us to form conjectures drawn solely from the nature of man and from the beings around him about what the human race might have become if left to itself. This is the question put to me, and what I propose to examine in this discourse. Since my subject concerns humanity in general, I will try to use a language suited to all nations—or rather, forgetting time and place, attending only to the men I am speaking to, I will imagine myself in the Lyceum of Athens, repeating the lessons of my masters, with Plato and Xenocrates as judges and the whole human race as audience.

O man, whatever your country may be and whatever your opinions, listen: here is your history, as I have thought to read it, not in the books of your fellow creatures, who are liars, but in nature, which never lies. Everything that comes from her will be true; nothing will be false except what I have involuntarily mixed in of my own. The times I am about to speak of are very remote: how much you have changed from what you once were! It is, so to speak, the life of your species I am going to describe, based on the qualities you have received, which your education and habits may have corrupted but cannot have entirely destroyed. There is, I feel, an age at which the individual man would wish to halt; you are about to inquire into the age at which you would have liked your whole species to stand still. Discontented with your present state, for reasons that promise your unfortunate descendants still greater discontent, you may perhaps wish you could go back; and this feeling should be a tribute to your first ancestors, a criticism of your contemporaries, and a warning to the unfortunates who will come after you.

chapters.title: Part 1
paragraphs: Important as it is, in order to judge the natural state of man correctly, to consider him from his origin and to examine him, as it were, in the embryo of his species, I will not follow his anatomy through its successive stages of development, nor pause to inquire what his animal system must have been at the beginning in order to become at last what it actually is. I will not ask whether his long nails were at first, as Aristotle supposes, only crooked talons; whether his whole body, like that of a bear, was covered with hair; or whether his walking on all fours, with his gaze fixed on the ground and limited to a horizon of a few paces, did not at once mark out the character and the limits of his ideas. On this subject I could form nothing but vague and almost imaginary conjectures. Comparative anatomy has so far made too little progress, and the observations of naturalists are still too uncertain, to provide a solid basis for reasoning. So, without recourse to the supernatural information given us on this point, and without regard to the changes that must have taken place in man's internal and external conformation as he applied his limbs to new uses and fed on new kinds of food, I will suppose that he has always been shaped as he appears today: walking on two legs, using his hands as we do, casting his gaze over the whole of nature, and measuring with his eyes the vast expanse of heaven.

If we strip this being, thus constituted, of all the supernatural gifts he may have received, and of all the artificial faculties he can only have acquired through a long process, and consider him, in short, exactly as he must have come from the hands of nature, we see in him an animal weaker than some and less agile than others, but, all things considered, the most advantageously organized of all. I see him satisfying his hunger at the first oak, quenching his thirst at the first stream, finding his bed at the foot of the same tree that supplied his meal—and with that, all his needs are met.

While the earth was left to its natural fertility, covered with vast forests whose trees were never mutilated by the ax, it would offer on every side both food and shelter to every species of animal. Men scattered among the rest would observe and imitate the industry of the beasts, and so rise to the level of their instincts—with the advantage that, while every species of beast was confined to a single instinct, man, who perhaps has none of his own, appropriated them all and lived on most of the various foods that other animals share among themselves. Thus he would find his subsistence much more easily than any of the rest.

Accustomed from infancy to the harshness of the weather and the rigor of the seasons, hardened by fatigue, and forced—naked and unarmed—to defend themselves and their prey from other wild animals, or to escape them by flight, men would acquire a robust and almost unchanging constitution. Their children, bringing into the world the excellent constitution of their parents and strengthening it through the very exercises that first produced it, would acquire all the vigor of which the human frame is capable. Nature, in this case, treats them exactly as Sparta treated the children of its citizens: she makes strong and robust those who come into the world well formed, and destroys the rest. This is different from our modern societies, where the state, by making children a burden to their parents, kills them indiscriminately before they are even born.

Since a savage man's body is the only instrument he understands, he uses it for various purposes that ours, for lack of practice, are incapable of. Our industriousness deprives us of the force and agility that necessity obliges him to acquire. If he had had an ax, would he have been able to break so large a branch from a tree with his bare arm? If he had had a sling, could he have thrown a stone so far? If he had had a ladder, could he have climbed a tree so nimbly? If he had had a horse, would he himself have been so swift on foot? Give civilized man time to gather all his machines around him, and he will easily beat the savage. But if you want to see a still more unequal contest, set the two of them naked and unarmed; you will quickly see the advantage of having all our resources always at our disposal, of being always ready for any event, and of carrying ourselves, as it were, perpetually whole and entire about us.

Hobbes claims that man is naturally fearless and bent only on attack and combat. Another famous philosopher holds the opposite, and Cumberland and Pufendorf also affirm that nothing is more timid and fearful than man in the state of nature: that he is always trembling, ready to flee at the slightest noise or movement. That may be true of things he doesn't know, and I have no doubt that he is terrified by every novelty presented to him when he can neither recognize the physical good or evil to expect from it nor compare his own strength to the dangers he is about to face. But such circumstances rarely arise in a state of nature, in which things proceed uniformly and the face of the earth is not subject to those sudden and constant changes brought about by the passions and caprices of bodies of men living together. Now, savage man, living dispersed among other animals and finding himself early on in a position to measure his strength against theirs, soon comes to compare himself with them. Perceiving that he surpasses them in skill more than they surpass him in strength, he learns to fear them no longer. Set a bear or a wolf against a robust, agile, resolute savage—as they all are—armed with stones and a stout club, and you will see that the danger will be at least equal on both sides; and after a few such trials, wild beasts, which don't like attacking each other, will not be at all eager to attack a man, having found him as wild and ferocious as themselves. As for animals that really do have more strength than man has skill, he is in the same situation as any other weaker animal, which nevertheless still manages to survive—except that he has the advantage that, being equally swift of foot and finding an almost certain refuge in every tree, he can take or leave the encounter at will, fighting or fleeing as he chooses. Add to this that no animal seems to make war on man naturally, except in self-defense or extreme hunger, nor displays any of those violent antipathies that would suggest one species was meant by nature to be food for another.

This is doubtless why Black Africans and savages are so little afraid of the wild beasts they may meet in the woods. The Caribs of Venezuela, among others, live in this respect in absolute security and without the smallest inconvenience. Though they are almost naked, Francis Correal tells us, they freely venture into the woods armed only with bows and arrows, yet no one has ever heard of any of them being devoured by wild beasts.

But man has other enemies, more formidable, against which he is not provided with such means of defense. These are the natural weaknesses of infancy, old age, and illness of every kind—sad proofs of our frailty. The first two are common to all animals; the last belongs chiefly to man in a state of society. Regarding infancy, it should be noted that the mother, carrying her child everywhere with her, can nurse it with much greater ease than the females of many other animals, which are forced to be constantly going back and forth, with great fatigue, one way to find food and another to suckle or feed their young. It is true that if the woman happens to perish, the infant is in great danger of perishing with her. But this risk is common to many other species whose young take a long time before they can fend for themselves. And if our infancy is longer than theirs, our lives are longer in proportion, so that in this respect things are roughly equal—though there are other rules to consider regarding the duration of the first period of life and the number of young, which don't bear on the present subject. In old age, when people are less active and perspire little, the need for food diminishes along with the ability to obtain it. The savage state also protects them from gout and rheumatism, and since old age is, of all ills, the one human aid can least alleviate, they cease to be without anyone noticing they are gone, and almost without noticing it themselves.

As for sickness, I will not repeat the vain and false declamations most healthy people pronounce against medicine. But I will ask whether any solid observations have been made from which it can be justly concluded that, in the countries where the art of medicine is most neglected, the average length of human life is shorter than in those where it is most cultivated. How could this be the case if we bring on ourselves more diseases than medicine can supply remedies for? The great inequality in ways of living—the extreme idleness of some, the excessive labor of others, the ease of stimulating and gratifying our sensual appetites, the too-rich foods of the wealthy, which overheat them and fill them with indigestion, and on the other hand the unwholesome food of the poor, often so poor in quality and so insufficient in quantity that they eat voraciously when they get the chance and overload their stomachs; sleepless nights, excesses of every kind, immoderate outbursts of every passion, fatigue, mental exhaustion, the countless pains and anxieties inseparable from every condition of life by which the human mind is constantly tormented—all these are far too clear proofs that most of our ills are of our own making, and that we could have avoided nearly all of them by keeping to the simple, uniform, and solitary way of life that nature prescribed for us. If she meant man to be healthy, I venture to declare that a state of reflection is a state contrary to nature, and that a thinking man is a depraved animal. When we think of the good constitution of savages—at least those we have not ruined with our strong liquors—and reflect that they suffer from hardly any ailments except wounds and old age, we are tempted to believe that in following the history of civil society we shall also be telling the history of human sickness. Such, at any rate, was the opinion of Plato, who inferred from certain remedies prescribed or approved by Podalirius and Machaon at the siege of Troy that several illnesses these remedies later gave rise to in his time had not yet been known to mankind. And Celsus tells us that the diet now so necessary was first invented by Hippocrates.

Subject, therefore, to so few causes of sickness, man in the state of nature has no need of remedies, much less of doctors. The human race in this respect is no worse off than other animals, and it is easy to learn from hunters whether they meet many infirm animals in the course of the chase. They certainly often come across some that bear the marks of having been seriously wounded, and many that have had bones or even limbs broken yet have healed without any other surgical help than time, or any regimen other than their ordinary life. Their cures seem to have been no less complete because they were not tortured by incisions, poisoned by drugs, or wasted by fasting. In short, however useful medicine may be among us when properly administered, it is certain that if the savage, when sick and left to himself, has nothing to hope for but from nature, he has on the other hand nothing to fear except from his disease—which often makes his situation preferable to ours.

We should therefore beware of confusing savage man with the men we see around us every day. Nature treats all the animals left to her care with a fondness that seems to show how jealously she guards that right. The horse, the cat, the bull, even the donkey, are generally taller, and always more robust, and have more vigor, strength, and courage when they run wild in the forests than when bred in the stall. By being domesticated, they lose half these advantages, and it seems as if all our care to feed and treat them well only serves to degrade them. It is the same with man: by becoming sociable and a slave, he grows weak, timid, and servile; his soft way of life completely saps his strength and courage. To this it can be added that the difference between savage and civilized man is even greater than between wild and tame beasts: for since men and beasts have been treated alike by nature, the many comforts in which men indulge themselves still more than they do their animals are so many additional causes of their deeper degeneration.

It is therefore not so great a misfortune for these primitive men, nor so great an obstacle to their preservation, that they go naked, have no dwellings, and lack all the superfluities we consider so necessary. If their skins are not covered with hair, they need no such covering in warm climates; and in cold countries, they soon learn to appropriate the skins of the beasts they have overcome. If they have only two legs to run with, they have two arms to defend themselves with and provide for their needs. Their children are slowly and laboriously taught to walk, but their mothers are able to carry them with ease—an advantage other animals lack, since the mother, if pursued, is forced either to abandon her young or to slow her pace to match theirs. In short, unless we suppose a singular and lucky concurrence of circumstances, which I will discuss later and which would be unlikely to occur, it is plain in every case that the first man who made himself clothes or a dwelling was supplying himself with things not at all necessary, since he had done without them until then, and there is no reason why he should not have been able to put up in adulthood with the same kind of life he had had in infancy.

Solitary, indolent, and constantly accompanied by danger, the savage cannot help being fond of sleep; and his sleep, too, must be light, like that of animals that think little and may be said to slumber whenever they are not thinking. Self-preservation being his chief and almost sole concern, he must exercise most those faculties most concerned with attack and defense—either for overpowering his prey or for keeping himself from becoming the prey of other animals. On the other hand, those organs that are perfected only by softness and sensuality will remain in a coarse and imperfect state, incompatible with any sort of refinement. So with his senses divided in this way, his touch and taste will be extremely coarse, while his sight, hearing, and smell will be exceptionally keen. Such, in general, is the animal condition, and such, according to travelers' accounts, is the condition of most savage nations. So it is no surprise that the Hottentots of the Cape of Good Hope can distinguish ships at sea with the naked eye at as great a distance as the Dutch can with their telescopes; or that the savages of America could track the Spaniards by smell as well as the best dogs could have done; or that these barbarous peoples feel no pain in going naked, or that they use large quantities of hot peppers with their food and drink the strongest European liquors like water.
So far I have considered only physical man; let us now look at him on his metaphysical and moral side.

I see in any animal nothing but an ingenious machine, to which nature has given senses with which to wind itself up and to guard itself, to a certain degree, against anything that might disorder or destroy it. I perceive exactly the same things in the human machine, with this difference: that in the operations of the beast, nature is the sole agent, whereas man has some share in his own operations, as a free agent. One chooses and refuses by instinct, the other by an act of free will. Hence the beast cannot deviate from the rule prescribed for it, even when it would be to its advantage to do so; while man, by contrast, often deviates from such rules to his own detriment. Thus a pigeon would starve to death beside a dish of the choicest meats, and a cat on a heap of fruit or grain, even though either might find nourishment in the foods it disdainfully refuses, if only it thought to try them. This is also why dissolute men run into excesses that bring on fevers and death: because the mind corrupts the senses, and the will keeps speaking when nature is silent.

Every animal has ideas, since it has senses; it even combines those ideas to a certain degree, and it is only in degree that man differs from the beast in this respect. Some philosophers have even maintained that there is a greater difference between one man and another than between certain men and certain beasts. So it is not so much understanding that constitutes the specific difference between man and beast as it is the human quality of free agency. Nature commands every animal, and the beast obeys her voice. Man receives the same impulse, but at the same time knows himself free to comply or resist. It is particularly in his awareness of this freedom that the spirituality of his soul is shown. For physics may explain, to a certain extent, the mechanism of the senses and the formation of ideas; but in the power of willing—or rather of choosing—and in the feeling of that power, nothing is to be found but acts that are purely spiritual and entirely inexplicable by the laws of mechanics.

But even if the difficulties surrounding all these questions still left some room for disagreement on this point between men and beasts, there is another very specific quality that distinguishes them and admits no dispute: the faculty of self-improvement, which, with the help of circumstances, gradually develops all our other faculties, and which is inherent in the species as in the individual. A beast, at the end of a few months, is all that it will ever be during its whole life, and its species, at the end of a thousand years, is exactly what it was in the first year of those thousand. Why is man alone subject to growing into a doddering old fool? Is it not because he is, in this, returning to his primitive state—and that whereas the beast, which has acquired nothing and therefore has nothing to lose, still retains the force of instinct, man, who loses, through age or accident, all that his perfectibility had enabled him to gain, falls thereby even lower than the beasts themselves? It would be a melancholy thing if we were forced to admit that this distinctive and almost unlimited faculty is the source of all human misfortunes; that it is this that, in time, draws man out of his original condition, in which he would have spent his days insensibly in peace and innocence; that it is this faculty that, by successively producing in different ages his discoveries and his errors, his vices and his virtues, makes him at length a tyrant both over himself and over nature. It would be shocking to be obliged to regard as a benefactor the man who first suggested to the Orinoco Indians the use of those boards they apply to the temples of their children, which secure to them at least some part of their imbecility and original happiness.

Savage man, left by nature to the sole guidance of instinct—or rather compensated for what he lacks by faculties capable at first of replacing it and later of raising him much above it—must accordingly begin with purely animal functions. Seeing and feeling must be his first condition, which he would share with all other animals. To will and not to will, to desire and to fear, must be the first and almost the only operations of his soul, until new circumstances cause new developments of his faculties.

Whatever moralists may say, the human understanding owes much to the passions, which, it is universally allowed, also owe much to the understanding. It is by the activity of the passions that our reason is improved, for we desire knowledge only because we wish to enjoy, and it is impossible to imagine why a person who has neither fears nor desires should bother to reason at all. The passions, in turn, originate in our needs, and their progress depends on that of our knowledge—for we can only desire or fear something on the basis of the idea we have of it, or from the simple impulse of nature. Now savage man, destitute of every kind of intelligence, can have no passions except those of the latter sort: his desires never go beyond his physical needs. The only goods he recognizes in the universe are food, a female, and sleep; the only evils he fears are pain and hunger. I say pain, not death, because no animal can know what it is to die: the knowledge of death and its terrors is one of the first things man acquires on departing from an animal state.

It would be easy, if necessary, to support this opinion with facts, and to show that, in all nations of the world, the progress of the understanding has been exactly proportionate to the needs people had received from nature, or had been subjected to by circumstances, and consequently to the passions that pushed them to provide for those needs. I could cite the arts rising in Egypt and expanding with the inundation of the Nile. I could follow their progress into Greece, where they took root afresh, grew up, and towered to the skies among the rocks and sands of Attica, while unable to germinate on the fertile banks of the Eurotas. I could note that in general the people of the North are more industrious than those of the South because they can't manage as well without being so—as if nature wanted to equalize matters by giving their understandings the fertility she had refused to their soil.

But without relying on the uncertain testimony of history, who does not see that everything seems to remove from savage man both the temptation and the means of changing his condition? His imagination paints no pictures; his heart makes no demands of him. His few needs are so easily met, and he is so far from having the knowledge needed to make him want more, that he can have neither foresight nor curiosity. The face of nature becomes indifferent to him as it grows familiar. He sees in it always the same order, the same successions; he has not enough understanding to wonder at the greatest miracles; nor is it in his mind that we can look for the philosophy a person needs in order to know how to notice, for once, what he sees every day. His soul, which nothing disturbs, is wholly wrapped up in the feeling of its present existence, with no idea of the future, however near at hand; and his projects, as limited as his views, hardly extend to the close of the day. Such, even today, is the extent of the native Caribbean's foresight: he will sell you his cotton bed in the morning without a thought, and come crying in the evening to buy it back, not having foreseen that he would want it again the next night.

The more we reflect on this subject, the greater appears the distance between pure sensation and the simplest knowledge. It is impossible to conceive how a man, by his own powers alone, without the aid of communication and the spur of necessity, could have crossed so great a gap. How many ages may have elapsed before mankind was in a position to behold any fire other than that of the heavens! What a multitude of chances must have come together to teach them the commonest uses of that element! How often must they have let it go out before they acquired the art of producing it again? And how often may such a secret have died with the man who had discovered it? What shall we say of agriculture, an art that requires so much labor and foresight, which is so dependent on others that it is clear it could only be practiced in a society that had at least begun, and which serves not so much to draw subsistence from the earth—for this it would produce of itself—as to force it to produce what most pleases our taste? But let us suppose that men had so multiplied that the natural produce of the earth no longer sufficed for their support (a supposition that, by the way, would prove such a life to be very advantageous for the human race). Let us suppose that, without forges or workshops, the tools of farming had dropped from the sky into the savages' hands; that they had overcome their natural aversion to continual labor; that they had learned to foresee their needs far enough ahead; that they had figured out how to cultivate the earth, sow grain, and plant trees; that they had discovered the arts of grinding corn and fermenting grapes—all things that must have been taught them by the gods, since it is inconceivable how they could have discovered them on their own. Yet even after all that, what man among them would be so absurd as to take the trouble of cultivating a field that might be stripped of its crop by the first comer, man or beast, that took a liking to it? And how could each of them resolve to spend his life in wearisome labor when, the more necessary the reward of his labor was to him, the surer he would be of not getting it? In short, how could such a situation lead men to cultivate the earth, until it had been regularly parceled out among them—that is, until the state of nature had been abolished?

Even if we were to suppose savage man as trained in the art of thinking as philosophers make him out to be; if we were, like them, to suppose him a thorough philosopher capable of investigating the sublimest truths and of forming, through highly abstract chains of reasoning, maxims of reason and justice deduced from the love of order in general or from the known will of his Creator; in a word, if we were to suppose him as intelligent and enlightened as he must have been—and, as a matter of fact, is found to have been—dull and stupid, what advantage would the species have gained from all such metaphysics, which couldn't be communicated from one person to another and would end with the one who came up with them? What progress could mankind have made while scattered through the woods among other animals? And how far could men improve or mutually enlighten one another when, having no fixed dwelling and no need of one another's assistance, the same persons hardly met twice in their lives—and perhaps then without recognizing one another or speaking together?

Consider how many ideas we owe to the use of speech, and how far grammar trains the understanding and facilitates its operations. Reflect on the inconceivable pains and the infinite space of time the first invention of languages must have cost. To these reflections add what came before, and judge how many thousand ages must have elapsed in the successive development, within the human mind, of those operations of which it is capable.

I will take the liberty here, for a moment, of considering the difficulties surrounding the origin of languages. On this subject I might content myself with a simple recap of Abbé Condillac's investigations, since they fully confirm my system and perhaps even first suggested it. But it is clear from the way this philosopher solves the difficulties he himself raises about the origin of arbitrary signs that he assumes what I question—namely, that some kind of society must already have existed among the first inventors of language. So while referring to his observations on this point, I think it right to give my own, in order to present the same difficulties in a light suited to my subject. The first that presents itself is to conceive how language could have become necessary at all; for since there was no communication among men and no need for any, we can conceive neither the necessity of this invention nor its possibility, if it was not somehow indispensable. I might claim, with many others, that languages arose in the domestic dealings between parents and their children. But this would not get around the difficulty, and would on top of that involve the same blunder made by those who, reasoning about the state of nature, always import into it ideas gathered in a state of society. Thus they constantly imagine families as living together under one roof, and the individuals of each as maintaining among themselves a union as close and lasting as that which exists among us, where so many common interests bind them. Whereas in this primitive state men had no houses, no huts, no property of any kind. Everyone lived where he could, seldom for more than a single night; the sexes united without design, as accident, opportunity, or inclination brought them together, and they had no great need of words to communicate their designs to each other; they parted with the same indifference. The mother nursed her children at first for her own sake, and afterward, when habit had made them dear to her, for theirs. But as soon as they were strong enough to seek their own food, they left her of their own accord. And as they had hardly any way of not losing each other other than remaining constantly within sight, they soon became quite incapable of recognizing one another when they happened to meet again. It is further to be noted that the child, having all his needs to explain, and therefore more to say to his mother than the mother could have to say to him, must have borne the brunt of the task of invention; the language he used would be of his own devising, so the number of languages would be equal to the number of individuals speaking them, and the variety would be increased by the wandering and roving life they led, which would not give time for any idiom to become settled. To say that the mother dictated to her child the words he was to use in asking her for one thing or another is an explanation of how already-formed languages are taught, but in no way explains how languages were originally formed.

But let us suppose this first difficulty is overcome. Let us imagine ourselves for a moment standing on this side of the vast gulf that must lie between a pure state of nature and the state in which languages had become necessary, and, granting their necessity, ask how they could first have been established. Here we have a new and worse difficulty to grapple with. For if people need speech to learn to think, they must have stood in much greater need of the art of thinking in order to invent the art of speaking. And even if we could conceive how the articulate sounds of the voice came to be taken as the conventional interpreters of our ideas, it would still remain to inquire what could have served as interpreters of this convention for those ideas which, corresponding to no sensible objects, could not be indicated either by gesture or by voice. So we can hardly form any tolerable conjectures about the origin of this art of communicating our thoughts and establishing a correspondence between minds—an art so sublime that, far distant as it is from its origin, philosophers still see it at such an immeasurable distance from perfection that no one is rash enough to affirm it will ever reach it, even if the revolutions time inevitably brings were suspended in its favor, even if prejudice were banished from our academies or condemned to silence, and those learned societies devoted themselves to this thorny question without interruption for whole ages.

The first language of mankind, the most universal and most vivid—in a word, the only language man needed before he had occasion to exert his eloquence to persuade assembled multitudes—was the simple cry of nature. But as this was prompted only by a kind of instinct on urgent occasions, to call for help in case of danger or relief in case of suffering, it could be of little use in the ordinary course of life, where more moderate feelings prevail. When men's ideas began to expand and multiply, and closer communication arose among them, they sought to invent more numerous signs and a more abundant language. They multiplied the inflections of the voice and added gestures, which are in their own nature more expressive and depend less on prior agreement for their meaning. Visible and movable objects were therefore expressed by gestures, and audible ones by imitative sounds. But since hardly anything can be indicated by gestures except objects actually present or easily described, and visible actions; since they are not universally useful—darkness or the interposition of a solid object destroys their effectiveness—and since besides they request rather than secure our attention, people eventually thought of substituting for them the articulate sounds of the voice, which, while not bearing the same relation to any particular ideas, are better calculated to express them all, as conventional signs. Such an institution could only be made by common consent, and must have been brought about in a way not at all easy for men whose coarse organs had not been accustomed to any such exercise. It is also in itself even harder to conceive, since such a common agreement must have had motives, and speech seems to have been highly necessary to establish the use of speech.

It is reasonable to suppose that the words first used by mankind had a much more extensive meaning than those used in languages already formed, and that, being ignorant of the division of speech into its constituent parts, they at first gave every single word the sense of a whole proposition. When they began to distinguish subject from attribute, and noun from verb—which was itself no common feat of genius—nouns were at first only so many proper names, the present infinitive was the only tense of verbs, and the very idea of adjectives must have developed with great difficulty, since every adjective is an abstract idea, and abstractions are painful and unnatural operations.

Every object at first received a particular name, without regard to genus or species, which these primitive originators were not in a position to distinguish. Every individual presented itself to their minds in isolation, as things are in the picture of nature. If one oak was called A, another was called B—for the primitive idea of two things is that they are not the same, and it often takes a long time for what they have in common to be seen. So the narrower the limits of their knowledge of things, the more copious their dictionary must have been. The difficulty of using such a vocabulary couldn't be easily removed; for to arrange beings under common, generic names, it became necessary to know their distinguishing properties. The need arose for observation and definition—that is, for natural history and metaphysics of a far more developed kind than men at that time can have possessed.

Add to this that general ideas cannot be introduced into the mind without the help of words, nor can the understanding grasp them except by means of propositions. This is one reason why animals cannot form such ideas, or ever acquire the capacity for self-improvement that depends on them. When a monkey goes from one nut to another, are we to imagine that he entertains some general idea of that kind of fruit, and compares its archetype with the two individual nuts? Certainly not; rather, the sight of one of these nuts recalls to his memory the sensations he received from the other, and his eyes, being modified in a certain way, give notice to the palate of the modification it is about to receive. Every general idea is purely intellectual; if the imagination meddles with it ever so slightly, the idea immediately becomes particular. If you try to trace in your mind the image of a tree in general, you never reach your goal. In spite of all you can do, you will have to see it as great or little, bare or leafy, light or dark; and if you were able to see in it nothing but what is common to all trees, it would no longer look like a tree at all. Purely abstract beings are perceived in the same way, or are only conceivable through language. The definition of a triangle alone gives you a true idea of it: the moment you imagine a triangle in your mind, it is some particular triangle and not another, and you cannot avoid giving it visible lines and a colored area. So we must make use of propositions and language in order to form general ideas. For as soon as the imagination ceases to operate, the understanding can only proceed with the help of words. If, then, the first inventors of speech could only give names to ideas they already had, it follows that the first nouns could be nothing more than proper names.

But when our new grammarians, by means I cannot conceive, began to extend their ideas and generalize their terms, the ignorance of the inventors must have confined this method within very narrow limits. And since they had at first gone too far in multiplying the names of individuals out of ignorance of their genus and species, they afterward made too few of these, from not having considered beings in all their specific differences. It would have required more knowledge and experience than they could have, and more pains and inquiry than they would have been willing to give, to carry these distinctions to their proper length. If even today we are continually discovering new species that have so far escaped observation, let us reflect how many of them must have escaped men who judged things merely from their first appearance! It is superfluous to add that the primitive classes and the most general notions must necessarily have escaped their notice as well. How, for instance, could they have understood or thought of the words matter, spirit, substance, mode, figure, motion, when even our philosophers, who have so long been making use of them, themselves have the greatest difficulty understanding them, and when, the ideas attached to them being purely metaphysical, no models of them are found in nature?

But I stop at this point, and ask my judges to suspend their reading a while, to consider that, after the invention of physical nouns—which is the easiest part of language to invent—there is still a long way to go before the thoughts of men will have found a perfect expression and constant form such as would meet the purposes of public speaking and have an effect on society. I beg them to consider how much time must have been spent, and how much knowledge needed, to discover numbers, abstract terms, the aorist and all the tenses of verbs, particles, syntax, the methods of connecting propositions, the forms of reasoning, and all the logic of speech. As for myself, I am so aghast at the mounting difficulties that present themselves, and so well convinced of the almost demonstrable impossibility that languages could owe their original institution to merely human means, that I leave to anyone who will take it up the discussion of this difficult problem: which was more necessary, the existence of society for the invention of language, or the invention of language for the establishment of society? But whatever the origin of language and society may be, it may at least be inferred, from the little care nature has taken to unite mankind by mutual wants and facilitate the use of speech, that she has contributed little to making them sociable, and has put little of her own into all they have done to create such bonds. It is in fact impossible to conceive why, in a state of nature, one man should stand more in need of another's help than a monkey or wolf needs another of its kind. Or, granting that he did, what motives could induce that other to assist him? Or even then, by what means could they agree about the terms? I know it is constantly repeated that man would, in such a state, have been the most miserable of creatures.
